hypotheses.builds_on: Reactive element effects known from superalloy studies (TXT::wikipedia::Superalloy::002 and ::012) and the importance of oxide scale continuity highlighted in the AlCoCrFeNi coating work (PMC10856430::web::009).
hypotheses.what_is_new: This hypothesis proposes using trace Ce addition—distinct from conventional Y additions—to tailor the oxide scale microstructure in a high-entropy refractory alloy, aiming to exploit nano-dispersion effects at the interface to improve oxidation resistance while preserving mechanical performance.

hypothesis.hypothesis: Incorporating a trace amount of cerium (≈0.2 at.%) into equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr will modify the native oxide scale by forming nano-dispersed CeO2 particles at the metal/oxide interface, thereby anchoring the scale and reducing its growth rate during high-temperature exposure.
hypothesis.material_initial_state: Equiatomic cast HfNbTaTiZr that forms a non-protective oxide scale during service in high-temperature air exposure, leading to degradation of oxidation resistance.
hypothesis.intervention: Dope the alloy with approximately 0.2 atomic % cerium during casting.
hypothesis.conditions: Exposure in air at 800–1000 °C for durations up to 100 h under tensile conditions similar to those of the baseline alloy.
hypothesis.structural_mediator: A modified oxide scale microstructure where dispersed CeO2 particles are present at the alloy/oxide interface, leading to reduced defect density in the oxide and enhanced adhesion.
hypothesis.mechanism: Cerium is known as a reactive rare earth element that, when present in trace amounts, segregates to the metal/oxide interface. In this alloy, Ce is expected to oxidize to CeO2 and form fine dispersoids within the native oxide scale. These dispersoids hinder the formation of fast diffusion paths (e.g., grain boundaries) and reduce the rate of scale thickening as well as spallation under thermal stresses. This reactive element effect, while well-established in superalloy systems, is tailored here to the unique oxide chemistry of a refractory Hf-based high-entropy alloy.
hypothesis.predicted_outcome: A measurable reduction in the oxidation rate will be observed, with oxide scale growth slowed and improved scale adhesion relative to the undoped alloy. Mechanical properties should remain essentially unaffected due to the low concentration of Ce. The quantitative improvement is uncertain but should be statistically significant compared to the baseline.
hypothesis.baseline: Undoped equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr that rapidly forms a non-adherent, quickly thickening oxide scale under high-temperature air exposure.
hypothesis.boundary: The addition is strictly limited to a trace (~0.2 at.%) level during casting; service testing is confined to air exposure at 800–1000 °C for up to 100 h and standard tensile loading conditions.
hypothesis.uncertainty: Though reactive element effects are documented, the specific effectiveness and interaction of Ce with the mixed oxides in HfNbTaTiZr are less well established, warranting further microstructural characterization.

falsification_experiment.design: Cast two sets of equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr samples—one doped with ≈0.2 at.% Ce and one undoped. Expose both to air at 900 °C for 100 h. Characterize the oxide scale using SEM/EDS and XRD to identify CeO2 dispersoids, quantify scale thickness and adhesion, and perform mechanical testing at room temperature and 1000 °C.
measurements: Detection and distribution of CeO2 within the oxide scale (SEM/EDS, TEM if possible)
Oxidation kinetics by measuring weight gain and oxide scale thickness
Mechanical property evaluation (tensile tests at room and high temperatures)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If Ce-doped samples do not show a statistically significant reduction in oxidation kinetics (e.g., similar scale thickness and poor adhesion) or exhibit degraded mechanical properties relative to the undoped samples, the hypothesis is falsified.

hypotheses.label: C1

source_paper.title: An oxidation resistant refractory high entropy alloy protected by CrTaO4-based oxide.

hypotheses.builds_on: Findings from the paper that attribute heterogeneous oxidation and defective oxide layers to the as-cast microstructure, combined with established superalloy processing principles that homogenization can improve oxidation behavior.
hypotheses.what_is_new: This hypothesis proposes a processing-route intervention (post-cast homogenization heat treatment) to improve the oxidation resistance of equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr, a strategy not pursued in the paper, thereby potentially enhancing oxide scale uniformity without altering the nominal composition.

hypothesis.hypothesis: Implement a post-casting homogenization heat treatment at an elevated temperature (e.g. 1200–1300 °C) to refine the microstructure of equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr, thereby promoting uniform diffusion and the formation of a more continuous and protective oxide layer upon subsequent high-temperature exposure.
hypothesis.material_initial_state: As-cast equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr with a dendritic microstructure that exhibits compositional heterogeneity leading to heterogeneous oxidation behavior.
hypothesis.intervention: Apply a homogenization heat treatment to the as-cast alloy at 1200–1300 °C for an optimized duration (e.g. several hours) to reduce chemical segregation and improve microstructural uniformity.
hypothesis.conditions: Post-treatment oxidation testing in air at 1000–1100 °C over 200 hours, along with mechanical testing at room temperature (tensile ductility) and at high temperature (yield strength).
hypothesis.structural_mediator: A more uniform and refined microstructure with reduced chemical segregation, leading to a homogeneous, continuous, and less porous oxide scale formation during oxidation.
hypothesis.mechanism: In the as-cast state, the dendritic microstructure promotes heterogeneous oxidation due to locally varying compositions, as observed in the paper. A homogenization heat treatment can eliminate or significantly diminish these compositional gradients. This enhanced uniformity facilitates more even diffusion of alloying elements during oxidation, promoting the formation of an oxide layer with fewer defects and gaps. A denser, coherent oxide scale reduces oxygen ingress, thereby improving oxidation resistance while minimally affecting the intrinsic mechanical properties.
hypothesis.predicted_outcome: A reduction in the oxidation rate (lower mass gain) and a more uniform oxide scale as evidenced by cross-sectional microstructural analysis. Mechanical property testing should show retention of ductility (8–16% at room temperature) and yield strength (163–530 MPa at 1000 °C) comparable to the untreated alloy.
hypothesis.baseline: The as-cast equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr alloy with its dendritic microstructure and non-uniform oxidation behavior.
hypothesis.boundary: This process is applicable for alloys intended for oxidation conditions in air at 1000–1100 °C with exposures up to 200 hours, provided that the heat treatment does not induce grain growth that could adversely affect mechanical properties.
hypothesis.uncertainty: The optimal heat treatment temperature and duration must be balanced to achieve homogenization without excessive grain growth, and the effect on oxidation resistance is predicted qualitatively.

falsification_experiment.design: Process a batch of equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr by homogenization heat treatment at 1250 °C for a selected period (e.g., 4 hours) and compare with as-cast samples. Subject both sets to oxidation testing in air at 1000–1100 °C for 200 hours, then perform microstructural characterization of the oxide scale (via SEM/EDS and XRD) and mechanical testing at room temperature and 1000 °C.
measurements: Oxidation mass gain curves
Microstructure and phase distribution of the oxide scale
Mechanical property assessments (tensile ductility and yield strength)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the homogenized alloy shows no significant improvement in oxide scale density or oxidation resistance, or if the homogenization detrimentally affects the mechanical properties compared to the as-cast state, the hypothesis is falsified.

hypotheses.label: C11

source_paper.title: Synthesis and Characterization of Multilayered CrAlN/Al2O3 Tandem Coating Using HiPIMS for Solar Selective Applications at High Temperature.

hypotheses.builds_on: The well-known beneficial effects of reactive element (Y) additions for oxide scale adhesion in high-temperature alloys (TXT::wikipedia::Superalloy::002) are tailored through controlled ion implantation and annealing to fit the specific context of equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr.
hypotheses.what_is_new: This hypothesis introduces a combined process of low-dose Y ion implantation with a post-implantation anneal specifically optimized to create a favorable Y distribution in equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr, addressing potential implantation-induced damage and enabling the formation of a more protective oxide scale—an approach not previously applied to this HEA.

hypothesis.hypothesis: Low-dose yttrium ion implantation combined with a controlled post-implantation annealing step can tailor the surface chemistry of equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr to promote the formation of a stable, adherent Y-enriched oxide scale during high-temperature exposure.
hypothesis.material_initial_state: Equiatomic cast HfNbTaTiZr that exhibits acceptable ductility and high-temperature strength but forms a non-adherent, rapidly growing oxide scale under high-temperature oxidizing conditions.
hypothesis.intervention: Perform low-dose yttrium ion implantation (targeting a concentration of a few atomic percent within the top 1–2 µm) followed by a mild post-implantation annealing treatment (e.g., 600 °C for 1 hour) to promote defect healing and controlled Y distribution near the surface.
hypothesis.conditions: Static air exposure at 800 °C for 5 hours, with subsequent mechanical testing at room temperature and elevated temperatures.
hypothesis.structural_mediator: A surface region with a controlled, homogenized Y concentration that encourages Y segregation at the oxide/alloy interface, thereby enhancing the adhesion and integrity of the oxide scale during high-temperature oxidation.
hypothesis.mechanism: Yttrium is a reactive element known to improve oxide scale adhesion by segregating to the metal-oxide interface, reducing scale spallation. The low-dose ion implantation introduces Y into the surface without significantly altering the bulk properties, while the subsequent annealing step heals implantation-induced defects and enables a controlled diffusion profile. Upon high-temperature exposure, this modified layer facilitates the formation of a coherent and protective oxide scale.
hypothesis.predicted_outcome: Y-implanted and annealed samples will develop a more adherent and slower-growing oxide scale, reflected in lower oxidation weight gain and fewer spallation events, with mechanical properties remaining similar to untreated samples.
hypothesis.baseline: Unmodified equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr forms a non-protective oxide scale with rapid oxygen ingress, and straightforward Y implantation without annealing risks surface embrittlement or damage.
hypothesis.boundary: The ion implantation dose must be low enough (e.g., a few atomic percent) and confined to the top 1–2 µm, with post-implantation annealing optimized to mitigate damage without triggering undesirable diffusion into the bulk; applicable for oxidation exposures at 800 °C for up to 5 hours.
hypothesis.uncertainty: Determining the optimal Y implantation dose and annealing temperature/time to balance oxide scale adhesion improvement and avoidance of surface damage; detailed concentration profiles and their effect on oxidation kinetics need experimental calibration.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr samples: one set undergoing low-dose Y ion implantation followed by post-implantation annealing, and another set left untreated. Expose both sets to air at 800 °C for 5 hours and characterize the oxide scale using SEM, TEM, and XPS. Perform oxidation weight gain measurements and mechanical tests (tensile testing) to compare properties.
measurements: Surface/interface composition and Y distribution (XPS, TEM/EDS)
Oxidation weight gain
Adhesion and spallation behavior of the oxide scale
Mechanical property tests (yield strength, ductility)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the Y-implanted and annealed samples do not show improved oxide scale adhesion (e.g., comparable or higher oxidation weight gain and spallation) or if mechanical properties are degraded relative to controls, then the hypothesis is falsified.

hypotheses.label: C6

source_paper.title: On the Microstructure and Properties of Nb-Ti-Cr-Al-B-Si-X (X = Hf, Sn, Ta) Refractory Complex Concentrated Alloys.

hypotheses.builds_on: This hypothesis builds on established principles that processing-induced microstructural refinement can influence oxidation behavior by reducing segregation and improving oxide scale uniformity. It extends those ideas to the specific case of equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr, whose complex composition may benefit from minimized diffusion pathways.
hypotheses.what_is_new: It proposes a single-processing intervention (rapid solidification) to directly engineer the microstructure and near-surface chemical homogeneity of equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr, a strategy that challenges the conventional cast state and has not been previously reported for this alloy system.

hypothesis.hypothesis: Modify the casting process via rapid solidification (e.g., melt spinning or laser surface remelting) to produce a significantly refined and more homogenized microstructure that suppresses macrosegregation and oxygen‐diffusion pathways, thereby enhancing oxidation resistance.
hypothesis.material_initial_state: Conventional equiatomic cast HfNbTaTiZr with a coarse-grained and moderately segregated microstructure that facilitates the formation of non-uniform and spallation-prone oxide scales during oxidation at high temperatures.
hypothesis.intervention: Apply a rapid solidification technique – such as melt spinning (for thin ribbons) or a localized laser surface remelting process – to the cast alloy. This treatment refines the grain structure, minimizes microsegregation and macrosegregation of reactive elements, and leads to a more uniform distribution of phases.
hypothesis.conditions: For melt spinning: rapid quenching from the melt to produce a thin ribbon sample; for laser surface remelting: use a controlled laser processing setup (with scan speeds and laser power chosen to remelt only the top 10–50 µm) under an inert gas atmosphere. Post-processing oxidation tests in air at 800 °C and 1200 °C for up to 5 hours; mechanical tests at room temperature and 1000 °C at strain rates between 10^–4 and 10^–2 s^–1.
hypothesis.structural_mediator: A highly refined, near-equiaxed, and homogenized microstructure featuring reduced grain sizes and diminished compositional gradients, particularly in the near-surface regions where oxidation initiates.
hypothesis.mechanism: Rapid solidification increases the cooling rate, limiting the time available for element segregation and coarse grain growth. A finer grain structure typically promotes a more uniform and adherent oxide scale by reducing pathways (e.g., grain boundaries, segregated pockets) that facilitate rapid oxygen ingress. In addition, a homogeneous distribution of constituents helps maintain the intrinsic oxidation resistance of each element and suppresses localized oxidation events (pesting).
hypothesis.predicted_outcome: The rapidly solidified alloy is expected to form a thinner, more uniform, and more adherent oxide scale upon high-temperature exposure, as reflected in lower oxidation mass gains and less spallation. Simultaneously, the refined microstructure should preserve – or even slightly enhance – the beneficial tensile ductility and high-temperature strength relative to the untreated, conventionally cast alloy.
hypothesis.baseline: Equiatomic cast HfNbTaTiZr produced by conventional arc melting and slow solidification, which exhibits microsegregation and coarse-grained structures leading to inadequate oxidation resistance.
hypothesis.boundary: The rapid solidification must be optimized so as to affect only the processing-induced microstructure without introducing detrimental residual stresses or causing loss of ductility; the beneficial microstructural state is targeted for use in oxidation exposures up to 5 hours at 800–1200 °C.
hypothesis.uncertainty: While refined microstructures are generally beneficial for oxidation resistance, the long-term thermal stability of the nanostructured layer at high temperatures is not fully predictable; grain growth during service could partially diminish the benefits.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of samples: one using rapid solidification (via melt spinning or laser surface remelting) and one set of conventionally cast specimens. Characterize the microstructure using SEM/TEM and measure grain size distributions and homogeneity (e.g., via EBSD). Subject both sets to isothermal oxidation in air at 800 °C and 1200 °C for 5 hours and measure oxidation mass gain and oxide scale morphology (using SEM/EDS, XRD). Perform tensile tests at room temperature and 1000 °C.
measurements: Grain size and compositional homogeneity (especially near the surface)
Oxidation kinetics (mass gain) and oxide scale integrity
Mechanical properties (yield strength, ductility)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the rapidly solidified specimens do not exhibit a significantly refined and homogenized microstructure, or if subsequent oxidation tests do not demonstrate a statistically improved (i.e., lower) oxidation mass gain and oxide scale integrity – or if mechanical properties are compromised compared to the conventional cast alloy – the hypothesis is falsified.
